topic.title: The handwritten note printed in lakhs
topic.claim: The 'note from our founder' in the box is the cheapest part of the packaging and the part that sells the next order.
topic.moment: You open a D2C parcel and find a cursive card that says 'Made with love, just for you'.

turn.believed: It's a personal touch from a small brand.
turn.actually: It's a printed card that makes a factory product feel like a gift from a person.

topic.because: People forgive a higher price when they feel they know who made it. A card costs a few rupees and buys that feeling.
topic.payoff: Try this: read the note from your last two D2C orders side by side.
topic.behaviour: D2C brands add founder notes and thank-you cards; buyers post unboxings and reorder.
topic.mechanism: A small story lets a brand charge for a feeling instead of the product.
topic.group: Online shoppers who buy from D2C brands
topic.send_to: The friend who keeps every cute card from every parcel.
topic.why_now: Almost every D2C brand now ships with the same kind of personal-touch insert.

score.why: The founder note card is a few rupees of printing that sells the next order. It's a behind-the-brand view of what D2C is selling.

topic.villain: a packaging tactic that manufactures a personal touch for a factory product

cover.headline: The founder's note is the [cheapest thing] in your parcel
cover.sub: And it's the part that sells your next order.

paragraphs: The founder's note is the cheapest thing in your parcel.
slides.why_swipe: How can the cheapest thing in the box be the thing that sells?

paragraphs: The parcel has been sitting outside your door since afternoon. You slit the tape with your house key and peel back the tissue paper, which crinkles like it's announcing something.
Under it, a note from the founder in loopy blue cursive. "Made with love, just for you." Signed with their first name, and a little heart.
slides.why_swipe: What does the card actually do to you?

paragraphs: And yes, it's sweet. The price had made you pause at checkout. Now it doesn't feel like paying a company. It feels like supporting a person.
The card goes into the drawer with the warranty slips. You'll never throw it away.
Run your thumb over the ink. It's flat and smooth and doesn't smudge, because it was printed.
The same card went into every box that week. Hundreds of signatures, and the founder's little heart never once got lazy.
**The cursive is a costume. It dresses a factory product up as a gift from a person.**
slides.why_swipe: Fine, it's printed. Does it actually change what you do?

paragraphs: Two months later you run out. A cheaper lookalike sits right there on Amazon. Your thumb hovers over Add to Cart.
Then you remember the card in the drawer, and buying the lookalike feels faintly like cheating on someone. You close the app and reorder from the brand that wrote to you.
slides.why_swipe: Why did a printed card beat a lower price?

paragraphs: A card costs a few rupees. Everything else in that box can be compared on price. The card is the only thing arguing against the comparison, and it never shows up on the bill.
**You don't feel tricked. You feel loyal, and that loyalty is what they were really selling.**
slides.why_swipe: How do you catch it happening to you?

paragraphs: Dig out the notes from your last two orders, from two different brands, and lay them side by side.
Look for what repeats. "Made with love." "Just for you." A first name. A little heart.
**Two founders who have never met, and somehow the exact same heart.**

end.save: Read it again the next time a parcel arrives with a card in cursive.
end.send: Send to the friend who keeps every cute card from every parcel.
end.promise: How brands really sell to you.

draft.caption: What's the most 'personal' card you've found in a parcel, and is it still in your drawer?
draft.alt_text: A text carousel. The cover reads: The founder's note is the cheapest thing in your parcel, and it's the part that sells your next order. The slides follow a reader opening a parcel and finding a note in loopy cursive, signed with a first name and a little heart, that says 'Made with love, just for you'. The price that made them pause now feels like supporting a person, and the card goes into a drawer. But the ink is flat and printed, the same card went into every box, and the founder's heart never got lazy across hundreds of signatures. Months later the reader nearly buys a cheaper lookalike on Amazon, remembers the card, and reorders from the brand. The card costs a few rupees and is the only thing in the box arguing against the price comparison. The reader doesn't feel tricked, they feel loyal, and that loyalty is what was being sold. The last slide asks the reader to lay notes from two different brands side by side and spot what repeats: made with love, just for you, a first name, a little heart. Two founders who have never met, and the exact same heart.
